title: Turning and flipping mattresses and bed-making
siteNotes: Which mattresses in the venue need turning or flipping, how often, and which are no-turn types (your manager will show you).
How heavy the mattresses are and which beds have handles (your manager will show you; no weight limit is quoted in this session).
Which beds are on raised bases or have wheels or glides, and which beds are best made as a pair (twin, king, super king).
Where the housekeeping trolleys and linen sacks are kept, and the manual handling risk assessment for housekeeping.
Who to report heavy or damaged mattresses to, and how pain or aches are logged (accident book or manager).
Confirm the venue's own rule that mattresses are always turned by at least two people, and that staff will not be penalised for reporting aches or damaged equipment (the session promises this).
legalNotes: Avoid, assess and reduce hazardous manual handling, and train people: Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 (https://www.hse.gov.uk/msd/manual-handling/index.htm and https://www.hse.gov.uk/pubns/books/l23.htm). Verified in HSE summaries.

Employers must assess risks and give health and safety training: Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999, regs. 3 and 13. Not re-checked online in this session; stated as per the session index.

HSE confirms back pain and other aches from manual handling are the most common type of work ill health, and has catering and hospitality MSD guidance (https://www.hse.gov.uk/catering/msd.htm). Verified by search summary.

Early reporting of aches and pains: HSE's MSD pages for workers cover symptoms and what to do (https://www.hse.gov.uk/msd/). The page itself could not be read in detail, so the advice to report early is good practice rather than a quoted rule.

NOT VERIFIED: HSE has no single housekeeping bed-making guide that I could read, so the specifics (team of two for bed-making, two or more people to turn a mattress, handles, keeping trolleys unloaded) are good practice drawn from the general principles of the Regulations, not quoted HSE rules. No weight limit is given, deliberately.
Please have the venue's own manual handling assessment for housekeeping confirm these techniques.

Review 6 Oct 2026 correction: the first draft said manual handling aches are 'the most common' work-related ill health. HSE's 2024/25 statistics put stress, depression or anxiety first (about 52% of cases) and musculoskeletal disorders second (about 27%, 511,000 workers), so the slide now says 'one of the most common causes'. 'Much of it is preventable' replaces 'Most of it'. 'Never lift or turn a mattress alone' and 'at least two people' are the venue's good-practice rule, not an HSE or statutory rule (the Regulations require assessment and reduction of risk, not a number of people); the GM should confirm this is the venue's policy and matches its own manual handling assessment.

cards.title: Turning and flipping mattresses and bed-making
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- make a bed without bending and twisting more than you need to
- turn a mattress as a team, never alone
- report heavy or damaged mattresses and early aches

cards.title: Beds are heavy work, every day
cards.body:
Making and turning beds means lots of bending, reaching and lifting, again and again. Small strains build up over weeks into back, shoulder and wrist problems.

> Muscle and joint problems, including back pain, are one of the most common causes of work-related ill health. Much of it is preventable.

items.title: Bending
items.text: Reaching over a low bed strains your back.

items.title: Repeating
items.text: One bed is fine. Twenty rooms add up.

items.title: Weight
items.text: Mattresses are awkward as well as heavy.

cards.title: Make it easy on your body
cards.body: Most of the strain comes from reaching and bending. A few habits take it away.

left.title: Do
items: Work in a pair on larger beds
Walk round the bed, tuck from each side
Bend your knees, keep your back straight
Keep sheets close to your body

right.title: Do not
items: Lift the mattress with one hand and tuck with the other

cards.title: Never lift or turn a mattress alone
cards.body:
A mattress is heavy, floppy and has no good grip. Turning one is a team job, whatever the size of the bed.

**Your manager will show you** which beds need turning, how heavy they are and which have handles.

items.title: Ask
items.text: Get at least one colleague before you start.

items.title: Clear
items.text: Strip the bed and clear the floor around it.

items.title: Lift together
items.text: Use the handles and agree a count.

items.title: Turn, lower
items.text: Move your feet to turn. Lower it slowly together.

cards.title: Do not twist, move your feet
cards.body:
Twisting your back while holding weight is a classic way to get hurt. Point your toes where the mattress is going and step round.

- Plan the move and agree who leads
- Keep the load close to your body
- Stop if it feels too heavy and ask for more help

items.title: Feet and hips
items.text: Turn with your feet, not your spine.

items.title: Load close
items.text: Keep it near your body and waist.

items.title: Twisting under load
items.text: Avoid it. This is where injuries happen.

cards.title: Let the trolley do the work
cards.body:
Use the trolley to move linen, not your arms. Keep the right things within easy reach so you do not stretch or bend.

- Keep the trolley unloaded of anything you do not need, and within reach of the bed
- Push, do not pull, and keep walkways clear
- Do not overfill linen sacks. Carry them close to your body, or wheel them

cards.title: Report early, stop if it hurts
cards.body: Pain is a warning. Telling someone early gets it sorted before it becomes a long-term problem. You will not be in trouble for reporting.

items.title: Heavy or damaged
items.text: Tell your manager about broken handles, sagging or very heavy mattresses.

items.title: Pain? Stop
items.text: Pause the task and tell your supervisor.

items.title: Take breaks
items.text: Rest between heavy tasks. Do not push on tired.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Never lift or turn a mattress alone
- Work as a team and agree each move
- Bend your knees and do not twist your back
- Use the trolley and keep it close
- Report heavy or damaged mattresses, and any pain, early

cards.q: You are on your own on a late shift and a guest's bed needs the mattress turned. What do you do?
options: Turn it yourself, slowly, as it is only one bed
Leave it and ask a colleague or supervisor to help you do it
Drag it to the edge, then flip it with a quick shove
Ask the guest to hold one end
cards.why: Mattresses are turned by at least two people. If nobody is free, wait. A guest is not trained or covered to help.

cards.q: To make a bed more safely, it is best to lean across it and tuck in both sides from one place.
cards.why: Leaning over strains your back. Walk round the bed, or work with a colleague on each side.

cards.q: Two of you are turning a mattress and a corner will not clear the bed frame. What is the safest move?
options: Twist your upper body to get it round
Pull harder while your colleague pushes
Move your feet to turn, or put it down and re-plan
Let the mattress drop onto the base
cards.why: Turn with your feet. If it does not clear, put it down and re-plan rather than twisting under load.

cards.q: Which TWO are good habits with your housekeeping trolley?
options: Pile it high to save trips
Keep what you need within reach of the bed
Pull it behind you through busy corridors
Push it and keep walkways clear
Leave it across the doorway
cards.why: Keep the right items close, push rather than pull, and keep routes clear. Overloaded trolleys are harder to move.

cards.q: Your lower back has felt sore after the last few shifts of bed turning. What should you do?
options: Carry on and see whether it passes
Tell your manager now so the task is supported
Wait until it is bad enough for time off
Only mention it if a guest notices you struggling
cards.why: Report aches early. Catching it early gives the best chance of stopping it becoming a long-term problem.

cards.q: A mattress handle has torn off, and you are due to turn that bed. What now?
options: Turn it carefully by yourself, using the other handle
Grip the edge hard and turn it with a friend
Report it and ask how to move it before turning
Skip the report, as it still turns fine
cards.why: Damaged mattresses or handles should be reported. Do not carry on with a faulty grip.

cards.q: The linen sack on your trolley is stuffed full and hard to lift. What is the best option?
options: Hug it to your chest and lift it quickly
Split it into two lighter sacks or wheel it
Drag it along the corridor floor
Throw it down the stairs
cards.why: Do not overfill sacks. Split the load, or wheel it, and keep it close to your body if you carry it.

cards.q: An ache in your back that eases overnight does not need reporting.
cards.why: Report aches early. Small problems are easiest to deal with before they build up.

cards.q: You need to make a large king-size bed in a rush. How is it best done?
options: Work with a colleague, one on each side
Lean over from one side and stretch
Lift the mattress one-handed and tuck
Kneel on the bed and pull the sheet
cards.why: Pairs on larger beds mean less reaching and less bending, for both of you.

cards.q: Taking short breaks between heavy tasks is a sensible way to cut the risk of strain.
cards.why: Rest helps your body recover. Do not push on while tired or in pain.
